newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arab states play normalisation - strongest card.
newsitem.headline: Arab states play normalisation - strongest card.

text.p: Arab states played their strongest card in a confrontation with Israel over Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem by threatening to backtrack on normal relations and restore the old economic boycott.

Arab foreign ministers meeting in Cairo agreed to recommend that their countries suspend normal relations with the Jewish state, close down any Israeli missions, reactivate the boycott and withdraw from multilateral Middle East talks.
But Egypt and Jordan, the two states which could have the greatest impact, appeared to be exempt from action because they have signed binding peace treaties with Israel.

"We were speaking about the latest steps taken by some Arab countries to normalise their relations. We didn't talk about those countries which signed peace agreements," said Farouk Kaddoumi, head of the PLO's political department.
"The draft was addressed to countries that have opened offices or sections in Israel in response to progress in the peace process," said Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.

The two ministers were referring to the tentative gestures other Arab countries such as Morocco, Tunisia, Oman and Qatar have made towards Israel since it reached its first agreement with the Palestinians three and a half years ago.
Moussa said it was up to individual countries how they put into practice the resolutions, which also remain subject to approval by their heads of state and government.
Israel, which started the latest crisis by starting building work on a new a settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa in Jerusalem this month, dismissed the resolution as absurd.
"Normal neighbourly relations and regional cooperation are supposed to be an asset and a common interest for all countries in this region," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Ygal Palmor.
"It is absurd that they are being deemed as a whip, so to speak, to be used against Israel whenever there is a crisis in the peace process."
Moussa said he had been in contact with U.S. Secretary Madeleine Albright but he gave no indication of how she felt about the decisions taken by the Arabs.
"The U.S. administration expressed its annoyance at developments in the peace process," he said. "She asked everyone to protect and salvage the peace process."

The United States angered the Arab states by vetoing two U.N. Security Council resolutions critical of Israel's settlement plan. Arab officials say this damaged Washington's role as a neutral sponsor of Middle East peace talks.

The final version of the Arab League resolution was not available on Sunday night but a draft in circulation earlier said the ministers favoured isolating Israel until it returned to what Arabs see as the basic principles of the peace talks.
The most important of these is land for peace -- the idea that the Arabs will make peace if Israel gives back the territory it captured in the Middle East war of 1967.
The territory includes East Jerusalem, annexed by Israel but seen by Palestinians as the capital of their future state.

"The council of the Arab League recommends stopping all normalisation steps which have been taken with Israel in the framework of the peace process and stopping to deal with it, including closing offices and missions," the draft said.
"(It recommends) suspending Arab participation in the multilateral talks and continuing to maintain the primary Arab boycott and reactivating it until just peace is achieved."
